content.title: What is the Object Class?
content.description: The Object class is the root (superclass) of the Java class hierarchy. Every class in Java directly or indirectly inherits from the Object class.

content.content: In Java, the Object class is the parent of all classes. It provides several built-in methods such as toString(), equals(), hashCode(), clone(), getClass(), wait(), notify(), and notifyAll(). These methods provide common functionality that every Java object can use.

content.title: Why is Object Class Important?
content.content: Since every Java object inherits from the Object class, its methods are available throughout the Java language, making them fundamental to object-oriented programming.
Inheritance from Object
If a class does not explicitly extend another class, Java automatically makes it inherit from the Object class.

content.title: Implicit Inheritance
Universal Parent Class
content.description: Every class in Java inherits the methods of the Object class, either directly or indirectly.

content.content: Important Methods of Object Class
The Object class provides several methods that support object comparison, string representation, cloning, runtime information, and thread communication.
The toString() Method
The toString() method returns a string representation of an object. It is commonly overridden to display meaningful object information.

content.title: toString() Example
Best Practice
content.content: Override toString() to display meaningful information instead of the default memory reference.
The equals() Method
The equals() method compares two objects for logical equality. By default, it compares object references, but it is commonly overridden to compare object contents.
The hashCode() Method
The hashCode() method returns an integer value representing an object's hash code. It is widely used in collections such as HashMap and HashSet.
The getClass() Method
The getClass() method returns the runtime class information of an object.
The clone() Method
The clone() method creates a copy of an existing object. A class must implement the Cloneable interface to support cloning.

content.content: Advantages of Object Class

items.question: Code Reusability
items.answer: Common methods are available to every Java object.

items.question: Standard Functionality
items.answer: Provides built-in methods for comparison, printing, and cloning.

items.question: Supports Collections
items.answer: Methods like hashCode() and equals() are essential for Java Collections.

content.content: Real-Life Analogy

content.title: Universal Identity Card
content.content: Every citizen receives a basic identity card with common information. Similarly, every Java object automatically receives the common functionality provided by the Object class.

content.title: Interview Importance
content.content: Questions about Object class methods, especially equals(), hashCode(), toString(), clone(), and getClass(), are extremely common in Java interviews.
Common Mistakes

items.question: Does equals() compare memory addresses?
items.answer: Not necessarily. It can be overridden to compare object contents.

items.question: Can clone() be used without Cloneable?
Should hashCode() be overridden when equals() is overridden?
items.answer: Yes. Both methods should follow the hashCode-equals contract.

content.title: Remember This
content.description: The Object class is the root of Java's class hierarchy. Every class inherits its methods, making them available to every object in a Java program.
